hunts.label: Thursday, Nov 26
hunts.subtitle: A howling, soaking holiday dawn: the squirrels are staying in bed, and so, wisely, should you.

rules.title: Storm morning: stand down at dawn
items: **No dawn hunt.** A wind advisory and a flood watch run until about 1 pm. Gusts near 40 mph, heavy rain, and possible thunderstorms make the pines dangerous.
**Optional afternoon sit** only after 1 pm, and only if: no thunder for 30 minutes, gusts are dropping, and nothing is coming down in the yard.
**Hunter orange is required** (deer gun season is open to Jan 1). Your deer is done, but others may be out after the storm.
**Crow is closed today.** Crow is Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday only.
No clock change before this hunt. All times are Eastern Standard Time.
rules.note: Friday morning after the front is the better hunt: drier air, hungry squirrels, and crow is legal again.

items: Before dawn: about **63F** and rising, after a low near 56F overnight.
9 am: no hourly figure. The day reaches about **72F**, so cool any game fast.
Wind: **E 17 to 22 mph, gusts to about 34 to 40 mph** in the morning (wind advisory). It turns **S 11 to 16 mph** in the afternoon, gusts near 30.
Rain: **90 percent.** Showers and possible thunderstorms before 1 pm, then only a slight chance 1 to 4 pm. About **1 to 2 inches** more rain today after 2 to 4 inches tonight. **Flood watch.**
Sunrise **6:55 am**. Legal light **6:25 am** (sunrise minus 30 minutes). Sunset **4:53 pm**.
Moon: **waning gibbous, about 90 percent**, two days past full. Rise and set times were not found.
conditions.meaning: Assumption: squirrels and rabbits hole up in heavy rain and strong wind, so the dawn hours will be nearly dead. When the rain stops and the wind falls, expect a burst of feeding, often in the afternoon. The bright moon adds some night feeding, which slows the morning even on a calm day.
conditions.hours_note: The hourly table was out of date this run, so there is no 4 to 9 am chart. Figures above come from the daily forecast text.

wind.label: S 11 to 16, gusts near 30 (afternoon window). Morning: E 17 to 22, gusts to 40.

in_season.tip: Dead in the storm. Watch for them as soon as the rain and wind ease.
Sits tight in thick, dry cover. Look on high ground, not near the swamp.
No covey seen here yet. Bonus only.
The swamp edge will be flooded. Skip it today; check new mud edges after the water drops.

in_season: Raccoon and opossum are open. Take only a sure, close shot.
Crow is closed on Thursdays. Bear is closed until Dec 12. Bobcat is open but you do not hunt it.
Deer: tag filled for the season. Do not shoot a deer.

plan.title: Storm stand-down, then the Dry Rise Seat
plan.why: The dawn hunt is called off. Tall pines on wet ground can drop limbs or fall in 40 mph gusts, and lightning is possible. If the storm clears after 1 pm, go to a new spot: the **highest dry ground in the west half of the loop, between the loop and the main trail**. Pick a seat under **shorter pines and holly, with no dead trees or hung-up limbs overhead**. Sit with your back to a live trunk, facing **north**. The afternoon sun is low in the southwest, behind your left shoulder, so it lights the trunks ahead of you. The south wind will carry your scent north, toward the squirrels. Squirrels trust eyes and ears more than nose, so stay very still. Rabbits come out of the low, flooded ground to dry cover, and high ground is where they will be. Every shot goes between NW and NE.

steps.text: Check the weather from the house. Storms and the wind advisory are on: stay in. Do the pack check, then enjoy the coffee.
Check the forecast again. Go only if the advisory has ended, there is no thunder for 30 minutes, and gusts are dropping. If not, skip today. Plan Friday morning instead.
Leave the yard on the main trail. Orange on, gun unloaded. Look up as you walk: note limbs hung in the canopy and trees across the trail. Go around, never under.
Reach the dry rise in the west half of the loop. Check overhead for dead wood. Sit against a live trunk, facing north. Load #4 with the plug in.
Seated watch. Listen for the first gnawing and the drip of cuttings. Scan trunks 20 to 40 yards out, NW round to NE. Wet squirrels look dark and sleek.
Unload. Walk the loop's thick edges slowly for rabbits. Kick, wait 30 seconds. Shots N, NE, or W only, ground behind.
Unload and count shells. Walk out on the main trail and do the land task.
Out at the yard, before the 4:53 sunset. Cool any game at once. It is a 72F day.

items: **In the gun: #4** (plug in). Squirrel and rabbit to 35 yards.
**Right pocket: #7.5** for a close rabbit or a quail flush.
**Slugs: zipped in a separate pocket.** Bear defense only.
**No 00 buckshot carried.**
**Choke: Modified.** Fine for everything today.
**.22 LR (optional):** head shots on a squirrel only, with a trunk or the ground certain behind it.
Pack - GRAB: gun, phone, water bottle filled, tell someone your plan and return time.
Pack - CHARGE: headlamp and spare flashlight before bed.
Pack - RESTOCK after the hunt: water, coffee or tea, nibble, nitrile gloves, .22 LR count, fatwood.
warnings: Never shoot a deer with birdshot. Not with #4, not with #7.5.
Rain can get into the action. Keep the muzzle down in rain and check the barrel for water or mud before you load.
Unload before crossing logs, ditches, or any downed tree. Fresh blowdowns roll and slip.

animals.name: Gray squirrel and fox squirrel
paragraphs: The most common game here. Grays work oaks, hickories, pines, and holly. A fox squirrel may show in the pines.
Today they stay in dens and thick boughs until the storm passes. The first calm hours after it are the best of the day.

details.title: Shot and load
steps: #4 at 20 to 35 yards, head and neck on a trunk squirrel.
With the .22: head only, wood or ground behind.
After the shot, wait 10 minutes. Mark the fall against two trees.

details.title: Technique: post-storm watch
steps: Wait until the drip from the trees slows.
Scan the ground first. Storms knock down cones and nuts, and squirrels come down to feed.
Then scan trunks low to high. A dark, sleek shape with a thin wet tail is a squirrel.

after: Tip: wind noise hides your movement but also hides theirs. Use your eyes more than your ears today.
Tip: never shoot a squirrel moving against the sky. Wait for it to stop on a trunk.

animals.name: Rabbit
paragraphs: Cottontails leave flooded low cover and move to dry, thick spots on higher ground. Look in holly, briars, and brush on the rise and around the bins.

details.title: Shot and load
steps: #4 or #7.5 at 15 to 25 yards, head and front shoulders.
Shoot only with the ground behind the rabbit.
Never shoot toward the south line or the field SE.

details.title: Technique: dry-cover check
steps: Look for the driest thick cover above the wet ground.
Stop 10 yards short. Kick the edge once and wait 30 seconds.
A rabbit that holds is looking at you. Find the eye, check the backstop, then shoot.

after: Tip: after heavy rain, fresh tracks in wet sand or mud show where rabbits moved to.

animals.name: Quail (bonus)
paragraphs: Northern bobwhite. No covey has been seen here, so this is a bonus. Wet coveys huddle in low, thick cover next to open ground.

details.title: Shot and load
steps: #7.5 in the right pocket is the quail load.
Pick ONE bird. Never shoot into the whole covey.
Shoot only birds flying N, W, or E. Let south-bound birds go.

after: Tip: wet birds sit tight and flush close. Be ready for a short, fast shot.

animals.name: Snipe
paragraphs: A migratory bird of soft mud edges. Today the swamp edge is under water, so skip it. When the water drops, the new mud margins can hold snipe. HIP registration and a 3-shell plug are required.

details.title: Shot and load
steps: #7.5, close and fast.
Let the zig-zag flight straighten, then shoot.
Shots N only over the swamp, never toward the house or field.

after: Tip: a raspy scaipe call as it flushes tells you it was a snipe.

animals.name: Raccoon and opossum
paragraphs: Both feed at night near the swamp and the bins. Rising water pushes them to high ground and hollow trees. See this week's skill.

details.title: Shot and load
steps: #4 to the head at 20 yards or less.
Approach from behind. Opossums play dead, so check before you handle.
details.note: Wear gloves. Rabies is possible in raccoons.

after: Tip: a raccoon abroad in daylight that acts tame or wobbly may be sick. Do not shoot it for meat. Back away.

animals.name: Bear and bobcat
paragraphs: Awareness only. Bear season is closed until Dec 12. Floods move animals, so watch the high ground. Give a bear space, talk out loud, and back away. Slugs are for defense only.

skill.title: Raccoon and opossum: identify, handle, skin, and decide on the meat
skill.principle: Know the animal by two features before you shoot, and treat every one as a disease carrier until it is skinned and cooked.

sections.title: Identify at dawn or dusk
steps: Look at the tail first. Raccoon: bushy, with dark rings. Opossum: thin, bare, and pale, like a rat's tail.
Look at the face. Raccoon: black mask across the eyes. Opossum: white face, long pink nose.
Look at the walk. Raccoon: hunched and rolling. Opossum: slow and waddling.
Check tracks. Raccoon: five long toes, like a small hand. Opossum: the hind foot has a thumb that points out to the side.
If you cannot name it by two features, do not shoot.

sections.title: Handle safely
steps: Wait 5 minutes after the shot. Approach from behind.
Touch the eye with a long stick. No blink means dead. Opossums play dead, so check twice.
Put on nitrile gloves. Never touch your face.
Do not touch raccoon droppings. They can carry roundworm eggs that harm people.
If the animal acted sick (tame, wobbly, out in daylight), do not keep it. Bag it with gloves and call the NCWRC helpline.

sections.title: Skin and clean
steps: Hang the animal by the hind legs.
Cut around each hind ankle, then down the inside of each leg to the vent.
Peel the skin down toward the head like a sock.
Open the belly and remove the insides. Do not cut the bladder or gut.
Find and cut out the small, bean-like glands under the front legs and inside the hind legs. They taint the meat.
Trim away the thick fat. It holds the strong flavor.
Rinse, cool on ice within the hour, and wash your hands and knife.

sections.title: Is the meat worth keeping?
steps: Young raccoon: yes, for many hunters. Dark meat. Slow-cook it (parboil, then roast or stew).
Opossum: edible but greasy. Many hunters pass. If you keep one, trim all fat.
Cook both well done, to at least 165F inside. These animals can carry parasites.

details.title: Why the glands matter
paragraphs: Raccoons have small, waxy glands in the fat under the legs and along the back. Left in, they give the meat a strong, musky taste. Cut them out whole.

skill.checkpoint: The next time you see a track or an animal at first or last light, name it raccoon or opossum by two features before you look closer. Send a note: with what you saw and the two features.

land.intro: A big storm is the best land lesson of the year. It shows you where water goes and which trees are unsafe.
steps: On the walk out, find the high-water mark at the swamp edge: a line of floating leaves and sticks. Pace it from the Junction.
Note any trail that went under water, and where.
Count new blowdowns and big hung-up limbs across or above the main trail and the loop.
Check your past sit trees for broken tops or dead limbs overhead. Strike any unsafe one from your list.
Send what you find with a note: message, for example: note: water rose 40 paces south of the Junction, 2 pines down on the loop, the holly seat has a hung limb.

safety: NEVER shoot south. The house is SW and the field is SE: no-shoot directions.
Every shot today goes between NW and NE, with the ground or a trunk behind the animal.
Do not enter the woods during the wind advisory or with thunder. If you hear thunder, unload and go to the house. Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.
Never sit or walk under dead trees or hung-up limbs. Wet ground lets whole pines tip over in gusts.
Stay off the flooded swamp edge. Water hides holes, stumps, and cypress knees.
Hunter orange hat and vest are required (Oct 17 to Jan 1). Deer gun season is still open for other hunters.
Sky shots only to the north.
